Open Parole?

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Victims of crime are increasingly calling for a review of South Africa's parole system. We investigate what is broken and why victims of crime deserve a say in whether offenders are paroled.

Unique Selling Point:
South Africa's parole system is seen as an endless trap for victims and surviving families. We speak to analysts who say the disadvantages of the current system often outweigh the benefits.

Summary:
For this story, we speaking to people who have a problem with South Africa’s parole process. As things stand, they say that the process is closed or not transparent - victims or surviving family members aren't involved up until the last stages of the process. They say it upholds the rights of the now convicted perpetrators over those of the victims, who must now participate in the process.

They say that the outcome is more often than not predetermined and in most cases the perpetrators still arent remorseful, or even showing signs of being rehabilitated. These are some of the issues that were raised by the family of Leigh Matthews, in a recent press conference. They have been working with the Women and Men Against Child Abuse. The organisation itself has been asssiting families who feel vulnerable during the parole process.




Further information:
On the day before her 21st birthday party, Leigh Matthews was abducted from the parking lot at Bond University in Johannesburg. Her parents received a call from the kidnapper, demanding a large sum of money. Her father paid, but 10 days later, there was still no sign of his daughter. This became one of the most publicised cases in South Africa and it seemed like everyone was looking for Leigh. On 21 July 2004, her body was discovered by a municipal worker cutting grass in the open velt next to the R81 Highway in, south of Johannesburg.She had been shot four times. Although she was found naked, she had not been sexually assaulted.
On 24 August 2004, police detective Superintendent Piet Byleveld took over the investigation. He identified 24-year-old Donovan Moodley as his prime suspect. Moodley was also a student at Bond University attended by Matthews, but was not acquainted with her
On 4 October 2004, Byleveld arrested Moodley outside his home in Alberton. Moodley appeared in the Randburg Magistrate’s Court facing charges of murch, kidnapping and extortion. On 25 July 2005, he pleaded guilty to all three charges in the Johannesburg High Court. Judge Joop Labuschagne found him guilty as charged, but ruled he had not acted alone in his judgement
Moodley was sentenced to Life Imprisonment for murder, 15 years for kidnapping and 10 years for extortion. He began serving his life sentence on 4 August 2005.
In his initial version of events, Moodley said he was driven by a need for money. He said he approached Matthews in the campus parking lot and asked her for a lift. They rode in her car together, where he then kidnapped her. Moodley said shortly after he extorted the R50,000 from her father he was unsure what to do with her, and then took her to a deserted field in Walkerville and shot her in the back of the head. He then burned his clothes to hide evidence.

FASTRACK TO 2021…

The family of Leigh Matthews is not happy with South Africa's parole processes. Her father, Rob, says the family was not informed at all about the pending parole hearing for her murderer, Donovan Moodley. The family says they still do not have any information from her convicted killer, Donovan Moodley, as to what happened during the period she was missing.

05 September 2021 - Carte Blanche HDTEST ACCOUNT10 September 2021

Press Release:


For Rob Matthews from Fourways, a life sentence for Donovan Moodley who had kidnapped and conspired to murder his daughter Leigh in 2004 brought a measure of comfort that justice had been served. In addition, parole rules had been strengthened, setting at 25 years the minimum period after which lifers should be considered for parole. But now, Matthews has discovered that, irrespective of serving a life sentence, Donovan Moodley may be eligible to appear before a parole board sooner than expected and far sooner than the Matthews family is prepared. This because of how cut-off dates for the application of the new parole regime have been determined by the courts. Carte Blanche investigates what’s at stake for families who are still living with the fallout of vicious crimes.

Script:


SCRIPT
VO – in 2004, the Matthews family from fourways, north of Johannesburg was catapulted into a kidnapping drama that felt like something straight out of a movie.
On the 9th of July, a day after her 21st birthday, Leigh was abducted from the parking lot of the Bond University campus in Sandton where she was a student, recalls her father, Rob Matthews.

SOUND UP - Rob Matthews
06:14 Those were 12 days of hell. Absolute hell. We didn’t sleep.

BONGANI LINK - (CLIP 2021.8.10 DAY ONE CARD 2) This is the home of Leigh Matthews childhood, it's the matthews family home. It is also here that Rob received the call from would-be kidnappers demanding a ransom. There is no price he would not pay to have his daughter back. And still till this day he’s fighting for justice.
The kidnapper contacted the family and demanded a ransom of R50 000 for Leigh’s safe return.

VO - Although he complied with the instructions, Rob Matthews would never see his daughter alive...

SOUND UP - Rob Matthews
07:02 - We got a call saying that they had found the body of Leigh. There are mixed feelings, you know. The feeling is that trauma has come to an end but now your next trauma in terms of who did it? Why? What was the reason? And that was just as chaotic.

VO - The mastermind behind the horrific ordeal was Donovan Moodley.
In 2005, he was handed a life sentence for the murder, a 15-year sentence for kidnapping and 10 years for extortion.

SOUND UP - Rob Matthews
10:36 It gave us a sense of closure because he got the harshest sentence available in the country and for that we had to be happy.
VO – That happiness was short-lived. Earlier this year, the Matthews family learned that Moodley is eligible to appear before a parole board sooner than expected.
According to the new parole regime, lifers SHOULD only be considered for parole after serving a minimum of 25 years in prison, NO LONGER 20 years - as was previously the case under the Correctional Services Act of 1959.
But Correctional Services Spokesperson Singabakho Nxumalo says the new parole rules were found to not apply to Moodley, because of two CASES THAT IMPACTED the minimum detention period convicted criminals have to serve before being considered for parole.

SINGABAKHO NXUMALO
21:16 right now Mr Moodley has served almost 16 years and his minimum detention period was on the 3rd of June 2018, for him to be considered for parole placement,

VO – The thought of Moodley’s potential release infuriates Rob Matthews. Leigh's father believes Moodley had accomplices, and says that Moodley's failure to name those who helped him is a sign that he feels no remorse for his crimes.

VO – The Correctional Services department requested the Matthews family to participate in a victim/offender dialogue. But Rob Matthews rejected the invitation as he believes Moodley will continue to conceal the whole truth.
BONGANI LINK (Clip 2021.8.11) - The whole parole process seems shrouded in mystery - it’s not an open system. The media may not attend. Rights organisations don’t attend. And sometimes the families of victims say they don't find out what's going on until it’s too late. It begs the question - what is the department of correctional services trying to hide?
VO - South Africa’s restorative justice process is offender-centric and doesn't not take the victims and affected families into consideration, says Luke Lamprecht of the human rights organisation Women and Men Against Child Abuse.

SOUND UP LUKE A victim offender dialogue in an alternative dispute resolution is a restorative process. Now there is nothing to restore between the Matthews’ family and Mr Moodley. The reason is you cannot restore that which you do not know. By all versions mr Moodley never made a full disclosure around the details of the murder

VO – The organisation calls for transparency in the parole system.

SOUND UP - LUKE LAMPRECHT
08:28 One, the system is closed. 2:they don't call for any expert evidence outside of their own system. So it’s a self-sealing system. Not transparent. 08:59 Why are we not transparent? That’s what concerns us.

VO - On the 20th of January 2003, Leigh Visser’s brother, 22 year old Warren was savagely murdered along with eight others at Sizzlers parlour in Sea Point, Cape Town.
The motive behind the massacre is still unknown, although it is widely believed a robbery was the reason why Adam Woest and Trevor Thys carried out the killings. They were handed nine life sentences for premeditated murder, 20 years for attempted murder and 15 years for robbery in 2004.
Thys died in 2008 and Woest is now eligible to be considered for parole.

SOUND UP - Leigh Visser
(Clip 2021.8.10) He slit their throats, hurt them crying, begging for their lives, doused them in petrol before shooting them twice execution style, not somebody that can be rehabilitated will do that. I fear that he will commit this again, given the freedom.

SOUND UP - Leigh Visser (06:37 Clip 2021.8.10) In South African life does not mean life. It really doesn't. He has barely served one life sentence.

07:02 ...fighting to keep a mass murderer in prison.doesn't even sound right. Keep a mass murderer in prison.

VO - Visser started an online petition in march this year calling for President Cyril Ramaphosa to look into the revisions of the Correctional Services Act.

BONGANI LINK - If Adam Woest and Donevan Moodley were convicted today it would take them longer to be eligible for parole. And that’s the nub of the problem. We have toughened up the laws to make it harder for them to get parole. But they were convicted before those changes were made.
VO - Forensic Psychologist Dr Gerard Labuschagne, who at the time of the Sizzlers massacre worked in the SAPS Investigative Psychology Unit, had access to the crime scene. He also interviewed Woest.

SOUND UP GERARD (Clip 0004.MXF)
10:10- I would have to say that anybody who commits a mass murder Is someone that should probably be never released to society cos we don’t really understand why they committed that crime. How do we fix that and say confidently and say let’s let them go and see what happens. The risks are too great.

VO - Labuschagne believes the parole system should incorporate an evidence based assessment that will give the parole board a full picture of the parolee. And forensic experts must be consulted.

GERARD LABUSCHAGNE
1:53 – ...I've heard a lot of horror stories that they don't often have the full details, they don't necessarily have a panel of experts that are present. I've heard for example that there will be two religious ministers that are present and if we are lucky a member of police on that particular panel to make a decision and those types of things concern me.

VO - Correctional Services Department Spokesperson Singabakho Nxumalo defends the current assessment procedures.

SOUND UP - SINGABAKHO
32:05 There is an assessment that we do. Hence then the issue of the correctional sentence plan 32:09 Hence then the specialists also coming into play making an assessment to check whether this inmate is indeed ready to be taken back into society so that if they are not satisfied that person will stay within a correctional facility.

BONGANI 32:24 But ultimately your assessment is based on what the inmate tells you….I mean who better to tell you who your people are than the victims of their crimes.
SINGABAKHO 32:39 No, no we have specialists employed who specialise in that area. I have mentioned psychologists, social workers and those are the people who will do our reports. Those reports go into the profile of an inmate.
BONGANI 33:29 Singabakho why is the parole system closed?
Singabakho 33:56 There is an option of a review. 33:55 Lets just say someone has been granted parole and lets say as a victim you’re not happy or other parties interested are not happy, they may approach the National Commissioner or even the minister will request that this parole placement be reviewed hence we even have the review boards.

34:34 Bongani ) Singabakho you and I both know that many victims simply don't have the resources to undertake the processes that you are talking about, which is why perpetrators who get out without their knowledge will often taunt them and say you can do nothing to me,

Zoom SINGABAKHO 33:52 It's not like a review you take to court, it's a review that you come to us and you don't have to pay any money for that.
VO - Nxumalo says the department is looking to implement a fully integrated system that’ll involve victims in their offender’s rehabilitation process while they’re serving their sentences. But for Rob Matthews, reconciliation is not a priority, justice is. He has vowed to continue fighting to ensure the man who killed his daughter remains in prison.

(Clip 0001.MXF) BONGANI 29:43 Do you get more angry?
I almost made this my life’s work. I had a really good job. And I just thought I’m not going to let this go. A lot of people have said let this go you’ll feel a lot better. I’m not the let it go kind of guy. He’s messed my family and I’m going to see this to the end.

Singabakho 33:56 There is an option of a review. 33:55 Lets just say someone has been granted parole and lets say as a victim you’re not happy or other parties interested are not happy, they may approach the National Commissioner or even the minister will request that this parole placement be reviewed hence we even have the review boards. 34:34 Bongani ) Singabakho you and I both know that many victims simply don't have the resources to undertake the processes that you are talking about, which is why perpetrators who get out without their knowledge will often taunt them and say you can do nothing to me, Zoom SINGABAKHO 33:52 It's not like a review you take to court, it's a review that you come to us and you don't have to pay any money for that. VO - Nxumalo says the department is looking to implement a fully integrated system that’ll involve victims in their offender’s rehabilitation process while they’re serving their sentences. But for Rob Matthews, reconciliation is not a priority, justice is. He has vowed to continue fighting to ensure the man who killed his daughter remains in prison. (Clip 0001.MXF) BONGANI 29:43 Do you get more angry? I almost made this my life’s work. I had a really good job. And I just thought I’m not going to let this go. A lot of people have said let this go you’ll feel a lot better. I’m not the let it go kind of guy. He’s messed my family and I’m going to see this to the end.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Victims of crime are increasingly calling for a review of South Africa's parole system. We investigate what is broken and why victims of crime deserve a say in whether offenders are paroled.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: South Africa's parole system is seen as an endless trap for victims and surviving families. We speak to analysts who say the disadvantages of the current system often outweigh the benefits.
metadata.Summary: For this story, we speaking to people who have a problem with South Africa’s parole process. As things stand, they say that the process is closed or not transparent - victims or surviving family members aren't involved up until the last stages of the process. They say it upholds the rights of the now convicted perpetrators over those of the victims, who must now participate in the process. They say that the outcome is more often than not predetermined and in most cases the perpetrators still arent remorseful, or even showing signs of being rehabilitated. These are some of the issues that were raised by the family of Leigh Matthews, in a recent press conference. They have been working with the Women and Men Against Child Abuse. The organisation itself has been asssiting families who feel vulnerable during the parole process.
metadata.Further information: On the day before her 21st birthday party, Leigh Matthews was abducted from the parking lot at Bond University in Johannesburg. Her parents received a call from the kidnapper, demanding a large sum of money. Her father paid, but 10 days later, there was still no sign of his daughter. This became one of the most publicised cases in South Africa and it seemed like everyone was looking for Leigh. On 21 July 2004, her body was discovered by a municipal worker cutting grass in the open velt next to the R81 Highway in, south of Johannesburg.She had been shot four times. Although she was found naked, she had not been sexually assaulted. On 24 August 2004, police detective Superintendent Piet Byleveld took over the investigation. He identified 24-year-old Donovan Moodley as his prime suspect. Moodley was also a student at Bond University attended by Matthews, but was not acquainted with her On 4 October 2004, Byleveld arrested Moodley outside his home in Alberton. Moodley appeared in the Randburg Magistrate’s Court facing charges of murch, kidnapping and extortion. On 25 July 2005, he pleaded guilty to all three charges in the Johannesburg High Court. Judge Joop Labuschagne found him guilty as charged, but ruled he had not acted alone in his judgement Moodley was sentenced to Life Imprisonment for murder, 15 years for kidnapping and 10 years for extortion. He began serving his life sentence on 4 August 2005. In his initial version of events, Moodley said he was driven by a need for money. He said he approached Matthews in the campus parking lot and asked her for a lift. They rode in her car together, where he then kidnapped her. Moodley said shortly after he extorted the R50,000 from her father he was unsure what to do with her, and then took her to a deserted field in Walkerville and shot her in the back of the head. He then burned his clothes to hide evidence. FASTRACK TO 2021… The family of Leigh Matthews is not happy with South Africa's parole processes. Her father, Rob, says the family was not informed at all about the pending parole hearing for her murderer, Donovan Moodley. The family says they still do not have any information from her convicted killer, Donovan Moodley, as to what happened during the period she was missing.
